pages.title: Properties of Matter and their Measurement
pages.text:
Definition: Physical properties can be observed or measured without changing the chemical identity of a substance.

Example / application: Examples include colour, density, melting point and boiling point.

Key takeaway: Physical properties can be observed or measured without changing the chemical identity of a substance.

pages.title: Physical and Chemical Properties
pages.text:
Definition: Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts to form new substances.

Example / application: For example, iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form rust; wood burns and forms new substances.

Key takeaway: Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts to form new substances.

pages.title: Measurement of Physical Properties
pages.text:
Definition: A measurement includes a numerical value and a unit.

Example / application: For example, 5 cm means five centimetres.

Simple explanation: Units make measurements clear and comparable.

Key takeaway: A measurement includes a numerical value and a unit.

pages.title: The International System of Units (SI)
pages.text:
Definition: Length: metre (m); mass: kilogram (kg); time: second (s); electric current: ampere (A); thermodynamic temperature: kelvin (K); amount of substance: mole (mol); luminous intensity: candela (cd).

Categories and characteristics: The SI base unit of mass is kilogram, although grams are common in chemistry.

Definition: Derived units combine base units.

Categories and characteristics: Area uses m^2; volume uses m^3; speed uses m s^(-1); density uses kg m^(-3); force uses newton (N), equal to kg m s^(-2).

Categories and characteristics: Chemistry also commonly uses litres (L), millilitres (mL) and grams (g).

Definition: kilo (k) = 10^3; centi (c) = 10^(-2); milli (m) = 10^(-3); micro (u) = 10^(-6); nano (n) = 10^(-9).

Categories and characteristics: Thus, 1 km = 1000 m, 1 cm = 0.01 m, 1 mm = 0.001 m, and 1 L = 1000 mL.

Key takeaway: Length: metre (m); mass: kilogram (kg); time: second (s); electric current: ampere (A); thermodynamic temperature: kelvin (K); amount of substance: mole (mol); luminous intensity: candela (cd).

pages.title: Mass and Weight
pages.text:
Definition: Mass measures the amount of matter.

Simple explanation: Its SI unit is kilogram (kg), though grams (g) are often used in chemistry.

Simple explanation: Mass does not change when an object moves from Earth to the Moon.

Simple explanation: Weight is gravitational force: W = m x g, where m is mass and g is gravitational acceleration.

Simple explanation: Weight is measured in newtons (N) and changes with gravity.

Key takeaway: Mass measures the amount of matter.

pages.title: Volume
pages.text:
Definition: Volume is the space occupied by an object or substance.

Simple explanation: Its SI unit is m^3.

Simple explanation: Useful conversions: 1 L = 1000 mL; 1 mL = 1 cm^3; 1 L = 1000 cm^3.

Simple explanation: For a box, volume = length x breadth x height.

Simple explanation: For an irregular solid that does not dissolve or react in water, the increase in water level after immersion equals its volume.

Key takeaway: Volume is the space occupied by an object or substance.

pages.title: Density
pages.text:
Formula / application: Density is mass per unit volume: density = mass / volume.

Terms and units: Common units are g cm^(-3), g mL^(-1) and kg m^(-3).

Worked example: Example: mass = 60 g and volume = 20 cm^3.

Formula / application: Density = 60 / 20 = 3 g cm^(-3).

Formula / application: Rearranging gives mass = density x volume and volume = mass / density.

pages.title: Temperature
pages.text:
Terms and units: Temperature indicates how hot or cold something is and is related to the average kinetic energy of its particles.

Terms and units: SI unit: kelvin (K).

Formula / application: T(K) = t(degrees C) + 273.15; t(degrees C) = T(K) - 273.15.

Worked example: Example: 27 degrees C = 300.15 K, approximately 300 K.

Practice: Rework the source example above. Explain each conversion and include the units at every step.

pages.title: Uncertainty in Measurement
pages.text:
Terms and units: No measurement is perfectly exact.

Terms and units: Instruments have limited precision.

Terms and units: A ruler marked only in centimetres cannot measure a length as finely as a ruler marked in millimetres.

pages.title: Scientific Notation
pages.text:
Terms and units: Write a number as a x 10^n, where a is at least 1 but less than 10.

Formula / application: Large number: 450000 = 4.5 x 10^5.

Formula / application: Small number: 0.00072 = 7.2 x 10^(-4).

Terms and units: The exponent tells how many places the decimal point moves.

Formula / application: Multiply the coefficients and add exponents: (2 x 10^3) x (3 x 10^4) = 6 x 10^(3+4) = 6 x 10^7.

Formula / application: Divide the coefficients and subtract exponents: (8 x 10^7) / (2 x 10^3) = 4 x 10^(7-3) = 4 x 10^4.

Terms and units: First make the powers of 10 the same.

Worked example: Example: 3 x 10^5 + 2 x 10^4 = 3 x 10^5 + 0.2 x 10^5 = 3.2 x 10^5.

Terms and units: Do not add or subtract exponents when adding or subtracting numbers.

Practice: Rework the source example above. Explain each conversion and include the units at every step.

pages.title: Significant Figures
pages.text:
Terms and units: All non-zero digits count: 347 has 3 significant figures.

Terms and units: Zeros between non-zero digits count: 1005 has 4.

Terms and units: Leading zeros do not count: 0.0042 has 2.

Terms and units: Trailing zeros after a decimal count: 2.500 has 4.

Terms and units: Trailing zeros in whole numbers can be ambiguous, so scientific notation can clarify precision: 1.5 x 10^3 has 2 significant figures; 1.500 x 10^3 has 4.

Terms and units: Round the final answer to the same number of significant figures as the input with the fewest.

Worked example: Example: 2.5 x 3.42 = 8.55, which rounds to 8.6 (2 significant figures).

Terms and units: Round to the least precise decimal place.

Worked example: Example: 12.11 + 3.2 = 15.31, which rounds to 15.3.

Terms and units: Keep extra digits in intermediate steps and round at the end.

pages.title: Dimensional Analysis
pages.text:
Terms and units: Use a conversion fraction equal to 1, arranged so unwanted units cancel.

Worked example: Example: 2.5 km x (1000 m / 1 km) = 2500 m.

Worked example: Example: 500 mL x (1 L / 1000 mL) = 0.5 L.

Terms and units: Check that the final unit matches the requested quantity.
